nameStory: Water-purslane gets its name from its love of wet places and its slightly fleshy, spoon-shaped leaves that resemble those of true purslane (a completely unrelated plant). The 'water' part is spot-on – this little plant thrives in marshes and muddy spots where its stems can root wherever they touch moist soil. It's also called spatula-leaf loosestrife because those tiny leaves really do look like miniature kitchen spatulas!
description: Water-purslane is a tiny, creeping annual that hugs the ground in wet places. This delicate plant produces hairless, reddish stems up to 10 inches long that sprawl along muddy surfaces, rooting at the joints like a natural ground cover. Its most distinctive feature is its collection of small, spoon-shaped leaves that feel slightly thick and fleshy to the touch. The whole plant has a low, mat-forming growth habit and often takes on reddish tones that help it stand out against muddy backgrounds.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny spoon or spatula-shaped leaves about half an inch long that feel slightly thick and succulent, arranged alternately along the stem with colors ranging from green to reddish

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Prostrate stems that lie flat against wet ground and root at the nodes (joints) wherever they contact moist soil, creating a creeping mat

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Solitary tiny flowers tucked in leaf axils (where leaves meet stem), often with minute white or pink petals, though some flowers may lack petals entirely

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, hairless stems up to 10 inches long with a distinctive reddish color, especially noticeable against dark mud

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round capsules containing extremely tiny seeds that develop after the inconspicuous flowers fade

habitat: Look for water-purslane in marshes, muddy pond edges, and other consistently moist areas where the soil stays wet or saturated. It thrives in the kind of boggy spots where your boots might sink in a bit, often growing alongside sedges, rushes, and other wetland plants. This European introduction is quite rare in New England, making any sighting special.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge in late spring as tiny reddish shoots that begin their ground-hugging spread across wet surfaces. Early leaves are often more reddish than green.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when the creeping stems reach their full length and the minute flowers appear tucked in leaf joints. Plants are most easily spotted now.
seasonality.fall: Plants complete their life cycle and die back, but seed capsules may persist briefly before releasing their tiny seeds for next year's growth.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground presence as this annual dies completely, surviving only as seeds in the mud waiting for spring warmth.

funFact: Water-purslane is an escape artist that can root and establish new plants from almost any stem segment that touches wet soil – it's like nature's version of a cutting that roots itself automatically wherever it lands!
confusionNotes: With only one recorded observation in New England, water-purslane might be confused with other small, creeping wetland plants like water chickweed or small pondweeds. Look for those distinctive spoon-shaped, fleshy leaves and reddish, rooting stems – no other wetland creeper quite combines these features.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, water-purslane isn't related to the common garden purslane that some people eat in salads. It belongs to the loosestrife family instead, making it a distant cousin of the infamous purple loosestrife. This adds to the confusion around common names in botany!
compareHints: Unlike its showy cousin purple loosestrife with tall spikes of magenta flowers, water-purslane is a ground-hugger with barely visible blooms. While purple loosestrife stands upright like a wetland sentinel, water-purslane sneaks along the mud surface like a botanical carpet. Both share the loosestrife family's tendency to thrive in wet places, but their growth forms couldn't be more different.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Purple loosestrife is the most common and showy of New England's Lythrum species.
Hyssop loosestrife is much smaller and more delicate than purple loosestrife, with tiny flowers versus showy magenta spikes.
Compared to purple loosestrife, winged loosestrife has the distinctive four-winged square stem, smaller individual flowers, and a much more delicate growth habit.
